chapters.title: Chapter 4: Calls, Covered Calls, and Collars

lessons.title: Put, Collar, or No Hedge: Comparing Your Choices Side by Side

children.text: You now have every tool this course teaches: protective puts, partial hedges, covered calls, collars, and the option of doing nothing at all. The hard part is no longer knowing how each one works. It is choosing between them for a specific portfolio, on a specific day, with a specific goal. This lesson puts all the choices on one table, with the same portfolio and the same three months, so you can see exactly what each one costs and what it buys. It also makes the case that for many investors the right answer is not an option at all.

body.text: There is no best hedge. There is only the structure that matches your tolerable drawdown, your horizon, your willingness to give up upside, and the price of protection today. Choosing not to hedge is also a decision, and it should be made as deliberately as any other.

children.text: The portfolio is the familiar one: ₹32,50,000 in Nifty 50 index funds, which is 130 units with the Nifty at 25,000. The horizon is three months. Every option premium below is the illustrative one used earlier in this course.

body.caption: The six choices, with their upfront cost

cells: Hold the funds and accept whatever happens
Buy 2 lots of the 24,000 put at ₹250
Buy 2 lots of the 22,500 put at ₹75
Buy the 24,000 put at ₹250 and sell the 26,500 call at ₹230, 2 lots each
Sell 2 lots of the 26,000 call at ₹390
Move ₹8,12,500 into a debt fund, no options at all
₹0, but tax may apply on the switch

body.caption: Result after three months at four Nifty levels (illustrative, ignoring taxes, dividends and charges)

body.title: Four of the choices compared across the same three months

children.text: Three things jump out of that table. The covered call barely helps in a crash: at Nifty 20,000 it saves only the ₹50,700 premium out of a ₹6.5 lakh fall. Cutting equity by a quarter reduces every outcome by a quarter, up and down, with no premium at all. And the collar produces the best crash result of any choice here, precisely because it sold away a rally it did not expect to need.

body.text: Notice what the far 22,500 put does. It costs less than a third of the near put and still cuts a 20% crash loss roughly in half, from ₹6.5 lakh to ₹3.35 lakh. It is nearly free in the flat case, costing just ₹9,750, and it barely dents the rally. For long-horizon investors who can live with a 10% fall but not a 25% one, cheap far-out protection is often the best value in this whole table.

children.text: Cost Per Rupee of Loss Avoided
Comparing premiums alone is misleading, because each structure buys a different amount of protection. A fairer measure is how much you pay for every rupee of loss it removes in a serious fall.

body.latex: \text{Cost per rupee protected} = \frac{\text{Upfront cost}}{\text{Loss avoided in a 20\% fall}}
body.caption: Loss avoided = the unhedged loss of ₹6,50,000 minus the loss under that choice
What each choice costs per rupee of loss avoided at Nifty 20,000

cells: No protection at all for the first 10% of a fall
All gains above 26,500, which is ₹1,95,000 at Nifty 28,000
All gains above 26,000, and almost no real protection
A quarter of every future rally, for as long as it lasts

body.text: The collar looks almost free on this measure, at about half a paisa per rupee protected, but that number hides its real price. At Nifty 28,000 the collar gives up ₹1,95,000 of gains, leaving it ₹1,65,100 behind the plain put once the premium saved is counted. Any comparison of hedges that ignores forgone upside will always flatter structures that sell options.

body.title: Loss avoided by the collar
body.prompt: At Nifty 20,000, the unhedged portfolio loses ₹6,50,000 and the collar loses ₹1,32,600. How much loss does the collar avoid, in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹6,50,000 − ₹1,32,600 = ₹5,17,400, for a net upfront cost of ₹2,600. The catch appears on the other side: above 26,500 the collar stops participating, so in a strong rally it gives up far more than it cost.

children.text: Matching the Structure to the Situation

cells: Long horizon, no near-term goal, still adding through SIPs
Falls help you accumulate, and premiums paid year after year are a large drag
Long horizon, but a deep crash would make you sell in panic
Cheap catastrophe cover that keeps you invested without eating returns
Hard goal within a year, tight tolerable drawdown, India VIX low
Buys a firm floor while keeping the upside, at a cost you can budget for
Hard goal within a year, but the premium feels too expensive
The call premium pays for the put, if you accept a capped gain
Want income from a holding you are content to sell higher
Premium income with a pre-agreed exit price, not protection
Too much equity for your stage of life, or portfolio under one lot
Fixes the cause rather than insuring the symptom, and costs no premium
Portfolio dominated by small cap or sector funds
Cut equity, or hedge only part and accept basis risk
A Nifty hedge cannot cover what the Nifty does not represent

body.title: Options hedge vs asset allocation change

columns.label: Hedge with options
points: Keeps your units, SIPs and long-term tax position intact
Protection is temporary and must be rolled, with a repeating cost
Keeps most of the upside, unlike selling out
Needs an F&O account, whole lots and monitoring
Leaves basis risk if your funds do not track the index

columns.label: Change the asset allocation
points: Removes the risk permanently with no premium
May trigger capital gains tax and exit loads
Reduces future returns as well as future falls
No lots, margin or expiry dates to manage
Works for any portfolio size, including small ones

body.label: The default answer
body.value: For most long-horizon investors, no hedge
body.context: Options cost money every quarter. They earn their keep when a real goal, a tight deadline or a genuine risk of panic selling is involved.

body.title: Pick the structure
body.question: Ramesh, 61, has ₹40 lakh in Nifty index funds and will withdraw ₹36 lakh in five months for a property purchase. India VIX is at 23, so protection is expensive, and he says he would accept a capped gain in exchange for a firm floor. Which fits best?
options: No hedge, since markets usually rise
A covered call, for the premium income
A collar, using call premium to pay for the put
A far out-of-the-money put about 15% below the market
body.explanation: His tolerable drawdown is only 10%, the deadline is fixed and puts are expensive at VIX 23. He has explicitly said he will accept a cap. That is the textbook case for a collar. A covered call gives almost no protection, and a far OTM put would leave the first 15% of a fall unprotected, which would already break his goal.

body.title: Timing the purchase
body.textWithBlank: Whatever structure you pick, protection is cheapest when India VIX is ___.
body.explanation: Implied volatility drives premiums. Deciding your hedging policy in a calm market, then acting on it, is how you avoid paying panic prices for the same protection.

body.title: Three investors, one market
body.scenario: It is a calm market. The Nifty is at 25,000 and India VIX is 12. Three investors ask you the same question: should I hedge? Aarti, 29, has ₹8 lakh in index funds, a ₹30,000 monthly SIP and no goals for 20 years. Dinesh, 48, has ₹60 lakh across index and flexi cap funds and no near-term goal, but he sold everything in March 2020 near the bottom and still regrets it. Shalini, 59, has ₹75 lakh in index funds and retires in eight months, when she will move ₹45 lakh into debt.
body.prompt: What would you recommend for each, and why?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Aarti: no hedge. Her portfolio is below one lot of exposure, so any Nifty option would be a large over-hedge. Her SIP benefits from falls and her horizon absorbs any drawdown. The right action is a written commitment to keep the SIP running.
2. Dinesh: a far out-of-the-money put, rolled a few times a year while India VIX stays low. He has no financial need to hedge, but he has proven behavioural risk. Cheap catastrophe cover, costing well under 1% a year at VIX 12, may be what keeps him invested through the next crash. His flexi cap holding adds basis risk, so the hedge should be sized on beta-weighted exposure and treated as partial.
3. Shalini: a near protective put on the ₹45 lakh she needs, not on the full ₹75 lakh. Her tolerable drawdown on that portion sets the strike, VIX at 12 makes protection cheap, and her deadline is fixed. A collar would also work if she wants the cost closer to zero and is happy to cap gains. She should also ask whether simply moving part of the ₹45 lakh to debt early is simpler, and compare the tax cost of doing that with the premium.
The lesson: same market, same day, three different right answers, driven by goals and behaviour rather than by any market view.

body.title: What about doing more than one thing at once?

children.text: These choices are not mutually exclusive, and sensible investors often blend them:
Move the goal money to debt and buy a cheap far put on what is left, so the goal is safe and the rest has catastrophe cover.
Hedge only half the beta-weighted exposure, which keeps the premium modest while cutting a crash loss meaningfully.
Collar one lot and leave the rest with a plain put, so only part of the upside is capped.
The rule is to keep it simple enough that you can state, in one sentence, what your worst case and best case are. If you cannot, the structure is too complicated for the job.

body.title: The decision sequence
steps: Name the risk: which rupees, by which date, and what happens if they are not there.
Ask first whether asset allocation solves it more cheaply than any option, after accounting for tax and exit loads.
If an option is right, calculate your tolerable drawdown and beta-weighted exposure, and size the hedge in whole lots.
Check India VIX and price at least two structures: a plain put and a collar, or a near strike and a far strike.
Write down the worst case, best case and total cost of your chosen structure in rupees, and only then place the order.

body.label: NSE Option Chain
body.description: Price two or three structures for the same expiry before choosing, so you are comparing real premiums rather than rules of thumb.

cards.definition: Upfront cost divided by the loss avoided in a given fall. Useful for comparing structures, but blind to forgone upside.
Cheap catastrophe cover that ignores ordinary corrections. Often the best value for long-horizon investors.
Near-zero upfront cost in exchange for all gains above the cap.
Protection equal only to the premium received, so it is income rather than a hedge.
Cutting equity reduces both downside and upside, with no premium but possible tax.
Choosing to carry the risk knowingly, after measuring it, rather than by default.

points: Compare structures on the same portfolio, over the same period, at the same set of index levels. Premiums alone tell you nothing.
A covered call saves only its premium in a crash. It is income, not protection.
A far out-of-the-money put is often the best value for long-horizon investors who only fear a catastrophe.
A near put buys a firm floor and keeps the upside. A collar buys the same floor far more cheaply, and pays for it with the rally.
Cutting equity removes risk with no premium, but costs tax and future returns.
Match the structure to your goal, deadline, tolerable drawdown and the level of India VIX, not to a market view.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. All premiums, returns and outcomes are illustrative and ignore taxes, dividends and transaction charges. The debt fund return assumption of about 6.5% a year is not guaranteed. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before choosing any hedging structure.
